analysis.one_liner: Charges oil, gas, and coal a rising fee, then pays every American a monthly cash dividend.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan carbon tax-and-dividend bill was introduced on December 19, 2018, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a fee on the carbon content of coal, oil, and natural gas, charged to the companies that produce or import them, starting at $15 per ton and rising by $10 every year. It would also charge a smaller fee on fluorinated greenhouse gases and add fees to imports and refunds for exports so U.S. companies are not undercut by countries without carbon rules. All of the money would go into a Carbon Dividend Trust Fund and be paid out monthly, in equal shares, to every U.S. citizen and lawful resident — one share per adult, half a share per child. The fee would be phased out once emissions fell below 10 percent of 2015 levels.
analysis.who_benefits: Most American households, especially lower-income ones, would receive equal monthly dividend payments funded by fees on fossil fuels. People living near coal plants and refineries would gain from cleaner air. U.S. steel, aluminum, cement, and chemical makers would get border refunds and import fees that protect them from competitors in countries without carbon pricing. Farmers would be exempted from fees on fuels used for farming, and companies that capture and store carbon dioxide would get rebates.

how_it_helps.text: Every citizen and lawful resident with a valid Social Security number would receive a monthly dividend — one full share for each adult, half for each child under 19 — paid from the fee revenue into a Carbon Dividend Trust Fund.
The carbon fee starts at $15 per ton in 2019 and rises by $10 each year, with a steeper $15 increase if emissions targets are missed, to push companies toward cleaner energy.
The first dividend would be paid in advance, in the month before the fee takes effect, so households get money before energy prices rise.

Border fee adjustments charge importers on carbon-intensive products like steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, and chemicals, and refund U.S. exporters, to prevent factories from moving overseas to dodge the fee.
Fuels used on farms for farming purposes would be exempt, and the dividend would not count as income for eligibility in any federal or federally funded assistance program.

analysis.who_pays: Producers and importers of crude oil, natural gas, and coal would pay the fee, and refineries, utilities, and other users would pass much of that cost through to consumers in the price of gasoline, heating fuel, and electricity. Households that drive long distances or use a lot of energy could pay more than their dividend returns. Fluorinated gas producers and heavy users would also face a new fee.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, gas, and coal producers and importers

drawbacks.text: The fee would raise energy prices — the CRS summary notes it is imposed on producers and importers of crude oil, natural gas, and coal, costs that businesses typically pass on to customers at the pump and on utility bills.
Dividend payments would be includible in gross income, so taxes would take back part of each payment for many households.
There is no dedicated transition help for coal miners and oil and gas workers or for communities built around those industries, whose employers would bear the fee directly.
The fee's annual increases end once emissions fall below 10 percent of 2015 levels, which critics could argue leaves long-term enforcement dependent on future Congresses rather than the fee itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is aimed squarely at ordinary households: the money from the fee comes back as an equal per-person dividend, which because it is the same for everyone is worth more to lower-income families than the price increases they bear, and the first payment is sent before the fee takes effect. The main real cost is to fossil fuel producers, energy workers, and higher-energy-use households, and the bill offers no targeted transition aid for the workers and regions that would absorb the heaviest hit. Whether the fee level achieves the emissions schedule is left to real-world results rather than guarantees, with an EPA review after six years.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate on December 19, 2018, and referred to the Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until Congress ended two weeks later.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Coons (D-DE) introduced the bill on December 19, 2018, joined by Sen. Jeff Flake (R-AZ).
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day it was introduced.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote appears in the bill's action history before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill would have charged fossil fuel producers and importers a carbon fee starting at $15 per ton, rising $10 annually, and deposited the revenue into a trust fund for equal monthly dividend payments to every citizen and lawful resident.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal producers and importers came out ahead: they would have paid the carbon fee under this bill, and the bill died without ever getting a hearing or vote. American households, who would have collected the dividends, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers that avoided the fee

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by one Democrat and one Republican, but because no hearing or vote ever occurred, no broader party positions were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and coal producers and importers
industries.note: They would pay the carbon fee, charged at $15 per ton rising $10 a year, on every ton of covered fuel they produce or import. Their loss is exactly what funds the public's dividend payments, and the bill died before the fee could ever take effect.

industries.industry: Carbon-intensive manufacturers (steel, aluminum, cement, glass, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: They would bear higher fuel costs, but the border adjustment refunds fees on their exports and charges importers on comparable foreign products, shielding them from countries without carbon pricing. Ordinary people pay more for energy but get dividends in return.

Facilities that capture and store carbon dioxide from fuels already subject to the fee would receive refunds equal to the fee on the captured tons, creating a direct revenue stream for the carbon-capture industry.

industries.industry: Fluorinated gas producers and industrial users
industries.note: They would face a fee on reported fluorinated greenhouse gas emissions set at 10 percent of the carbon fee rate, a smaller but real new cost aimed at potent refrigerant and industrial gases.
